strengths: Soundness: The paper presents an unusually extensive empirical investigation, combining prompt and persona variations, checkpoint comparisons, layer sweeps, activation patching, mean ablation, sparse-feature interventions, and held-out-concept evaluation. The bidirectional steering and projection/residual swap experiments convincingly challenge the narrow hypothesis that detection is controlled by one linear direction.

Originality and significance: Mechanistically analyzing concept-injection self-reports is timely and potentially important. The proposed evidence-carrier/gate decomposition and steering-attribution framework offer interesting hypotheses and tools beyond prior behavioral demonstrations.
The distinction between detection and forced identification is useful, and their different layer profiles help separate willingness to answer affirmatively from concept readout.

Several causal results are substantive: layer-45 MLP interventions change detection, ablating fewer than 200 selected gate features lowers detection from 39.5% to 10.1%, and patching them into controls raises it to 25.1%. The learned vector is evaluated on 100 concepts excluded from training and reports zero false positives in that setting.
Presentation: The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually polished. Definitions, prompts, representative responses, hyperparameters, and many appendix analyses are supplied.

Limitations and ethics are treated thoughtfully. The paper explicitly avoids claims about consciousness, acknowledges model- and architecture-specificity, discusses judge bias and unresolved attention mechanisms, and identifies anthropomorphism, refusal bypass, and misleading self-report as dual-use risks.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is not established. Refuting a single linear direction does not show that the model performs introspective anomaly detection: a multidimensional out-of-distribution response to large residual-stream perturbations, coupled to ordinary affirmative-response circuitry, predicts many of the same findings. The paper lacks decisive matched controls such as norm- and layer-matched random perturbations, semantically scrambled vectors, natural activation shifts, and diverse non-introspection yes/no questions.

The gate analysis is partly circular. Gate candidates are selected for negative direct attribution to the Yes-minus-No logit and are then interpreted as an anomaly-detection circuit because their ablation changes Yes/No reports. That intervention establishes control of the response token, but not that these features compute whether an internal state is anomalous. Their max-activating examples are primarily generic negation and answer-boundary features, which reinforces this alternative.

Evidence carriers are selected using dose, detection, identification, and gate-connectivity criteria and largely evaluated on the same concepts. With hundreds of thousands of candidates and no clearly separated feature-discovery/test split, the causal and correlational evidence is vulnerable to selection bias. Ablating roughly 441,000 carriers is also too broad to support a specific circuit interpretation without reconstruction-error and matched-random-feature controls of comparable intervention magnitude.

The claim that post-training installs an introspection circuit is stronger than the evidence. Base models differ in instruction following, chat formatting, calibration, and default Yes/No behavior; weaker activation of instruct-model-derived gate features does not isolate introspection-specific learning. The OLMo trajectory mainly shows that DPO suppresses false positives while leaving very low true-positive rates.

The learned steering-vector experiment directly optimizes injected examples toward an affirmative templated answer and controls toward a negative one; Appendix N indeed finds a generic YES direction. Generalization to held-out concepts from the same task demonstrates task-level behavioral generalization, but does not by itself reveal greater latent introspective capacity. Side-effect evaluation mainly measures response length rather than task accuracy, calibration, harmfulness, or refusal rates.

Reliance on a single GPT-4.1-mini judge is not accompanied by human validation, inter-rater agreement, or sensitivity to alternative graders. This is material because coherence and concept-match judgments define outcomes used throughout the mechanistic analyses.

Statistical reporting is incomplete in places: the construction of several confidence intervals is unspecified, repeated generations within concepts may not be independent, and extensive layer, strength, direction, and feature searches invite researcher-degree-of-freedom effects. The selected layer and strength appear optimized on the same 500-concept collection used for major conclusions.

Reproducibility is mixed. The manuscript gives many useful procedural details and uses public models/transcoders, but the provided PDF ends the code-availability sentence without a repository link. Exact feature-selection thresholds, random seeds, confidence-interval procedures, abliteration weights, judge validation, and full evaluation data are insufficient for independently reproducing the strongest results.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper presents an unusually extensive mechanistic investigation of concept-injection detection, combining behavioral tests, activation patching, ablation, transcoder features, and a new steering-attribution analysis.

Soundness: Several results use direct causal interventions rather than correlations alone. In particular, the localization of detection effects near the layer-45 MLP and the gate-feature ablation/patching experiments provide meaningful evidence about how the model produces its reported answer.

The experiments cover 500 concepts and include prompt variants, dialogue formats, base/instruct checkpoints, an abliterated model, and limited checks on Qwen and OLMo. The opposite-direction and component-swap experiments also offer useful evidence against a strictly one-dimensional account.

Presentation: The manuscript is polished, well organized, and rich in informative figures. It generally distinguishes detection from identification and provides unusually substantial appendices and prompt details.

The limitations and ethics discussions appropriately acknowledge model-family dependence, judge bias, anthropomorphism, and dual-use risks. I found no unresolved ethical issue that independently prevents acceptance.
weaknesses: Soundness/construct validity: The central interpretation as an introspection-specific anomaly detector is not established. Detection is operationalized as giving an affirmative answer to an explicit yes/no question, while the identified gates are features for tokens preceding “no,” and the learned vector contains a generic “YES” direction. The paper does not run the decisive matched controls: applying the same injections and interventions to unrelated questions with default-negative answers, alternative reporting schemes without yes/no outputs, or comparable non-concept perturbations. Consequently, the results remain compatible with a prompt-conditioned affirmative-response mechanism rather than introspective awareness.

The claimed behavioral robustness is overstated. Some prompt variants and nonstandard roles produce large false-positive rates, and performance under the conservative variants is only moderate. The OLMo pipeline is especially weak evidence for emergence: after DPO/instruction tuning, TPR is only 2.9%/0.9%, despite 0% FPR. Base-versus-instruct comparisons also confound introspection with instruction following, chat formatting, calibration, and willingness to adopt the prompted persona.

The mechanistic feature analysis is highly adaptive. Gates and carriers are selected using attribution, dose-response, detection, identification, and gate-connectivity statistics closely tied to the same task and data on which their behavior is characterized. There is no clearly separated discovery/test split across concepts, prompts, or output formulations. Ablating hundreds of gates or roughly 441,000 carriers also risks large off-manifold interventions, so these results do not cleanly identify a compact introspection circuit.

The statistical protocol is insufficiently specified for the volume of adaptive analysis. Many figures report 95% intervals without defining the resampling unit or accounting for repeated generations nested within concepts. There is little treatment of multiple comparisons or selection effects from choosing layers, strengths, thresholds, directions, and top-ranked features. The GPT-4.1-mini judge is not validated against human labels or an independent judge, although its classifications feed most downstream analyses.

The learned steering-vector result does not demonstrate additional latent introspective capacity. It is trained directly on task-specific affirmative and negative target sentences and evaluated on held-out concepts but essentially the same task and prompt distribution. Appendix N itself shows a generic affirmation direction; zero FPR on the original controls and response-length checks on generic prompts do not rule out a conditional answer-style shortcut.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the reproducibility statement ends with “code is available at” but provides no repository or artifact. Key results therefore cannot currently be independently checked, particularly the feature-selection pipeline, intervention implementation, judge outputs, random seeds, uncertainty calculations, and learned steering vector.

Significance: The narrower finding—that residual injections interact with distributed semantic features and late yes/no response circuitry—is potentially useful. However, the paper repeatedly elevates this into claims about “genuine anomaly detection,” an “introspective circuit,” and latent introspective capacity. Those central claims require new controls and held-out validation, so the weaknesses outweigh the paper’s considerable technical merits in its current form.

strengths: Soundness is supported by unusually broad triangulation: 500 concepts, prompt and persona variations, injection-layer sweeps, base/instruct/abliterated checkpoint comparisons, and causal ablation and patching experiments. The convergence of behavioral, geometric, and mechanistic evidence is persuasive.

The paper directly tests an important alternative explanation—that detection is driven by one affirmative-response direction—using projection/residual swaps, bidirectional steering, orthogonal directions, and cross-validated prediction. These experiments provide meaningful evidence for a higher-dimensional nonlinear mechanism.

The localization of detection to MLP computation, followed by the identification of late-layer gate features and distributed upstream evidence carriers, is technically interesting. Necessity and partial-sufficiency interventions make the circuit account substantially stronger than a purely correlational feature interpretation.

The steering-vector experiment provides a notable held-out result: large improvements in detection and joint introspection on 100 unseen concepts while retaining zero measured false positives. This supports the practically significant conclusion that default prompting under-elicits task performance.

The work is original and potentially significant for mechanistic interpretability and the study of model self-reports. The steering-attribution formulation and its feature-level graphs are useful methodological contributions beyond this particular task.

Presentation is clear and exceptionally thorough, with informative figures, full prompts, examples, hyperparameters, and substantial appendices. The limitations, ethics, and broader-impact discussions appropriately distinguish this controlled behavior from consciousness and acknowledge anthropomorphism, manipulation, and refusal-bypass risks.
weaknesses: Most mechanistic evidence comes from Gemma3-27B. Qwen is used only for prompt robustness, while the OLMo post-training result has very low final sensitivity. Consequently, the specific gate/carrier circuit and its claimed installation by post-training are not yet established as general phenomena across model families.

The term “introspective awareness” remains stronger than the evidence warrants. The experiments establish task-specific detection of an artificial residual-stream perturbation under an explicit injection prompt; they do not establish faithful access to naturally occurring beliefs, goals, uncertainty, or other internal states. “Internal anomaly detection” is the better-supported interpretation.

The conclusion that the capability is absent before post-training is partly confounded by elicitation: base models lack an applicable chat template and are evaluated with plain-text role formatting. Comparable TPR and FPR show failure on this protocol, but do not rule out latent pretraining representations or a capability accessible through another readout.

Central behavioral labels rely on GPT-4.1-mini, yet the paper reports no human audit, inter-rater agreement, alternative-judge comparison, or judge-error sensitivity analysis. This is especially important for permissive semantic judgments such as “closely related concept” and for distinguishing coherent detection from steering-induced discourse.

Feature discovery and validation splits are insufficiently specified. Gates and carriers appear to be selected using correlations or attributions closely related to the evaluated outcomes, and several circuit demonstrations focus on selected features and concepts. Independent discovery/evaluation splits would reduce circularity and better quantify how often the proposed circuit generalizes.

Simultaneously editing hundreds of thousands of non-orthogonal transcoder features is difficult to interpret as clean feature ablation: summed decoder interventions may introduce reconstruction and off-manifold effects. This particularly weakens the quantitative evidence for the highly distributed carrier population, although the concentrated gate interventions are more convincing.

The learned vector contains a generic affirmative direction and is evaluated across steering layers on the held-out concepts, apparently using that set to identify the best layer. Its side-effect analysis mainly measures response length rather than task accuracy, calibration, unusual affirmative claims, and comprehensive safety behavior, so the claim that it merely reveals latent capacity is somewhat stronger than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete in the manuscript: sample sizes, resampling units for confidence intervals, seeds, and selection protocols are missing for several plots, and the reproducibility statement ends with “code is available at” without an actual link. These omissions should be corrected before publication.

strengths: The paper makes an original and significant contribution by moving beyond behavioral demonstrations of concept-injection detection to a mechanistic account separating detection from concept identification.

The empirical program is unusually broad: 500 concepts, prompt and persona variations, multiple model families and training stages, refusal ablation, objective-level DPO controls, activation patching, feature interventions, and held-out evaluation of the learned bias vector.

Several causal results are compelling. Layer-45 MLP ablation and patching respectively reduce and induce detection, the effect is absent in the base model but retained after refusal ablation, and gate-feature interventions show substantial necessity and partial sufficiency.

The post-training study is well controlled relative to typical checkpoint comparisons: shuffled and reversed DPO, chosen/rejected SFT, no-reference DPO, margin-plus-KL, and domain ablations support a role for contrastive preference learning rather than simple exposure or KL regularization.

The paper is clearly organized and visually polished, distinguishes detection, identification, and introspection metrics, and generally calibrates its interpretation by acknowledging that the setup is artificial and does not establish consciousness or broad self-knowledge.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: prompts, judge rubrics, sampling settings, training hyperparameters, cross-validation procedures, feature resources, concept lists, and code availability are described. The ethics and broader-impact discussion appropriately addresses misleading self-reports, refusal bypass, and dual-use concerns.

The downstream audit of the learned bias vector is particularly valuable and candid: it shows negligible general self-knowledge benefit and substantial degradation of chain-of-thought faithfulness and prefill detection, preventing the elicitation result from being overstated.
weaknesses: The strongest mechanistic claim—a two-stage evidence-carrier-to-gate circuit—is less firmly established than the gate result alone. Evidence carriers are selected using correlations and connectivity on the analyzed data, individually have weak effects, and require ablating up to roughly 441,000 transcoder features to obtain a large behavioral change. Such massive interventions may introduce transcoder reconstruction error, feature crosstalk, or off-manifold effects, and the circuit-selection analysis lacks a clean held-out validation set.

The identified gates are predominantly generic features preceding negative or affirmative answers at the final prompt token. Their causal role convincingly explains the model's Yes/No output decision, but does not by itself show that they implement introspective anomaly detection rather than a task-specific response-policy pathway. Stronger controls using non-binary reporting tasks, unrelated questions, and norm-matched random or non-concept perturbations would sharpen this distinction.

The claim that contrastive preference optimization enables introspection is demonstrated mechanistically only indirectly and behaviorally mainly through one OLMo training trajectory. Official checkpoints differ in more than the named stage, while the controlled LoRA replications yield relatively modest discrimination—especially on Gemma. Replication across additional fully documented training trajectories would be needed to establish generality.

Some analyses involve potentially circular selection. In particular, the success/failure threshold is chosen to maximize linear separability in concept-vector space before reporting cross-validated classification, and gate/carrier features are selected using statistics closely related to the outcomes on which they are intervened. Nested selection or independent concept splits would provide cleaner estimates.

Statistical reporting is incomplete. The manuscript repeatedly reports 95% confidence intervals without specifying their construction or resampling unit, despite trials being nested within concepts. It also performs large-scale feature searches without discussing multiple-comparison or selection effects. Claims of 0% false positives should include denominators and upper confidence bounds.

The behavioral labels rely entirely on GPT-4.1-mini, but no human validation, inter-rater agreement, or sensitivity analysis with alternative judges is reported. Because coherence and ambiguous detection statements directly determine the central metrics, judge error could systematically affect comparisons.

The principal mechanistic experiments rely on Gemma3-27B and Gemma Scope transcoders, limiting generalization. Applying an instruct-model transcoder to base and abliterated checkpoints also assumes a stable shared feature basis that is not quantitatively validated.

The learned bias-vector gains should not be interpreted as amplified general introspection: the vector contains an affirmative-response direction and substantially harms other self-monitoring tasks. The authors disclose this clearly, but it narrows the significance of that intervention to the specific concept-injection protocol.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript combines unusually broad behavioral experiments with causal interventions. It evaluates 500 concepts, prompt and persona variants, injection-layer and strength sweeps, component patching/ablation, and held-out concepts for the learned bias vector. The projection/residual swaps and bidirectional steering experiments provide useful evidence against a single-direction explanation. Significance: Understanding why models report activation interventions is relevant to interpretability and oversight. The separation between detection and forced identification, and the finding that targeted elicitation does not improve broader self-knowledge, are particularly useful observations.
Originality: The training-stage comparison, proposed evidence-carrier/gate account, and steering-attribution framework constitute a novel mechanistic treatment of a recently reported phenomenon.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. It provides extensive appendices, concrete response examples, full task and judge prompts, and an unusually candid limitations discussion.

Ethics: The authors appropriately avoid claims about consciousness, identify dual-use and refusal-bypass risks, and report adverse downstream effects of the learned bias vector, including degraded chain-of-thought faithfulness and prefill detection.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation: The experiments establish sensitivity to activation perturbations, but do not establish that the model performs introspective anomaly monitoring. The reported mechanism suppresses features that promote the default answer “No”; this is also a direct output-bias or causal-bypass mechanism. The paper does not perform the decisive control of measuring whether the same injections suppress negative answers or increase affirmative answers on unrelated matched yes/no questions, despite discussing this alternative in the related work.

Soundness—circuit claims: The evidence does not justify the strong description of a localized, two-stage circuit whose components are “necessary and sufficient.” Ablating the layer-45 MLP only reduces detection from 39.0% to 24.2%, and patching it yields only partial recovery. Evidence-carrier interventions require hundreds of thousands of selected features, while gate interventions are chosen specifically for negative direct-logit attribution. These results support partial mediation through response-related features, not necessity, sufficiency, or a well-delimited circuit.

Feature discovery and testing appear insufficiently separated. Gates and carriers are selected using attribution, dose-response, detection, identification, and connectivity criteria on the same experimental distribution on which their interventions are evaluated. Without held-out concepts/trials and selection-aware controls, the causal effect sizes can be inflated. Intervening on roughly 441,000 carrier features also raises substantial off-manifold and reconstruction concerns.

The claim that the circuit is absent in the base model is weakly supported because Appendix N applies transcoders trained on the instruct model to every model variant. A weaker activation pattern in this potentially mismatched feature basis does not demonstrate absence. Moreover, DPO is studied behaviorally in OLMo, whereas the proposed circuit is chiefly studied in Gemma instruct versus base; the paper never shows that DPO creates the claimed gate/carrier mechanism.

The conclusion that contrastive preference optimization is the primary driver is too strong. The custom finetuning comparisons apparently use single runs, with no across-seed uncertainty, and the official checkpoints differ in more than one controlled variable. The Gemma LoRA-DPO replication produces only a +4.6-point effect versus +38.2 points for the official instruct model, underscoring that the result does not explain the main model behavior.

Behavioral robustness is overstated. Some prompt/persona variants produce substantial false positives, and Appendix B.3 acknowledges that false-positive behavior depends systematically on trial numbers; the headline 0% FPR is restricted to trial numbers 1–10. The paper should evaluate randomized identifiers, broader control prompts, non-concept and norm-matched random perturbations, and unrelated question types.

The learned bias vector is presented as exposing latent introspective capacity, but Appendix R identifies a generic “YES”/assertiveness direction, and Appendix S shows degraded chain-of-thought faithfulness and prefill detection. This evidence supports narrow task-specific response calibration at least as well as enhanced introspection. The main claims should be revised accordingly rather than treating zero FPR on held-out concept names as decisive.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the reviewed manuscript: the code and model links are blank, the LLM judge is not validated against human annotations or alternative judges, and several uncertainty calculations, feature-selection thresholds, and intervention details are insufficiently specified. The compute-intensive use of 27B–235B models and 262k-feature transcoders further limits independent verification. Overall, the work has clear merit, but central mechanistic and introspection claims require stronger controls and more cautious framing before acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript provides unusually broad converging evidence for the phenomenon in the reviewed paper :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/9d63dd30ce4443c9afd4624531151958/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}. Behavioral tests span 500 concepts, multiple prompts, dialogue formats, checkpoints, injection layers, and model families; the mechanistic claims are supported by activation patching, ablation, probing, feature interventions, and integrated steering attribution rather than correlational visualization alone.

Soundness: The training-stage study is especially thoughtful. Official OLMo checkpoints are complemented by controlled LoRA experiments comparing DPO, shuffled/reversed preferences, SFT, reference-free DPO, margin-based contrastive training, and domain ablations. These results make a credible case that contrastive preference optimization contributes to detection behavior.

Originality: The proposed evidence-carrier-to-gate account is a novel and useful mechanistic picture. The finding that distributed early features converge on a small collection of later default-negative features goes materially beyond prior behavioral demonstrations of steering awareness.

Significance: Establishing how models detect internal activation interventions is relevant to interpretability and safety. The separation between detection and concept identification, the relationship with refusal mechanisms, and the post-training analysis offer insights likely to motivate follow-up work even if the term “introspection” remains debatable.

Presentation, reproducibility, and ethics: The paper is clear, visually polished, exceptionally thorough, and candid about its artificial setting and limited generality. Prompts, concept-vector construction, sampling parameters, training objectives, hyperparameters, judge rubrics, and intervention formulas are documented. The downstream audits showing that the learned bias vector degrades chain-of-thought faithfulness and prefill detection are particularly responsible. The ethics and dual-use discussion is proportionate and does not overclaim consciousness or subjective experience.
weaknesses: The strongest interpretive claim—a two-stage anomaly-detection circuit—is somewhat ahead of the evidence. The identified gates are generic features immediately preceding negative answers, so intervening on them can directly alter the Yes/No response policy without establishing that they specifically compute anomaly detection. Conversely, the proposed evidence carriers require ablation of roughly 441,000 features to reduce detection from 38.6% to 13.8%, and patching all carriers reaches only about 10.5% detection. This supports a distributed pathway but not yet a compact or complete circuit explanation.

The experiments do not include the most decisive behavioral controls against an affirmative-response confound: matched non-concept or random perturbations, and alternative questions whose correct answer remains “No” under the same injected vectors. Anti-reward and prompt variants help, but most central measurements still use the same explicit injection framing and Yes/No report. The appendix also notes systematic confabulation for trial numbers outside 1–10, which qualifies the headline robustness and 0% false-positive claims.

The claim that introspection “emerges specifically” from contrastive preference optimization should be softened. Training conditions appear to be represented by single runs, with reported uncertainty mainly arising from evaluation samples rather than training seeds. The LoRA effect on Gemma is modest compared with the official instruct checkpoint, and sequential public checkpoints differ in more than an isolated objective. The evidence supports DPO as sufficient to induce some discrimination, but not as the uniquely identified cause of the full capability.

All behavioral labels depend on GPT-4.1-mini, yet no human-labeled audit, inter-rater agreement, or judge sensitivity analysis is reported. Because judge outputs define detection rates, success/failure partitions, and several downstream mechanistic targets, systematic errors could propagate through much of the analysis. This is a notable reproducibility and measurement weakness despite the publication of judge prompts.

The mechanistic conclusions largely rest on Gemma3-27B and on pretrained Gemma Scope transcoders; using the instruct-model feature basis across base and abliterated variants may complicate comparisons. The paper appropriately acknowledges limited architecture/model generality and unclear attention mechanisms. It also claims that code is available, but the anonymized manuscript shows no accessible code URL, preventing verification during review. These limitations reduce reach but do not outweigh the paper’s substantial technical contribution.
